content: Garlic is believed to possess antimicrobial and antiviral properties that may help alleviate symptoms of the common cold, among other potential health benefits. Garlic supplements are widely used, and the common cold is a condition associated with significant health burdens and economic costs. On average, children experience six to eight colds annually, while adults typically have two to four. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether garlic (Allium sativum) is effective in preventing or treating the common cold when compared to placebo, no treatment, or other standard treatments. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, OLDMEDLINE, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and AMED, covering studies published up to August 2014. The review focused on randomized controlled trials that compared garlic with placebo, no treatment, or standard treatments for the prevention or treatment of the common cold. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the studies, selected relevant trials, and extracted data for analysis. From the search, eight trials were identified as potentially relevant. However, only one trial met the inclusion criteria. This trial involved 146 participants who were randomly assigned to receive either a garlic capsule containing allicin (dose unspecified) or a placebo once daily for 12 weeks. The results showed that the garlic group experienced 24 episodes of the common cold, compared to 65 episodes in the placebo group (P < 0.001). Additionally, the total number of illness days was lower in the garlic group (111 days) compared to the placebo group (366 days). However, the time to recover from a cold was similar between the two groups, with an average of 4.63 days in the garlic group and 5.63 days in the placebo group. The trial relied on self-reported episodes of the common cold but was considered reasonably well-conducted in terms of randomization and allocation concealment. Adverse effects reported in the garlic group included rash and a noticeable odor. The authors concluded that there is insufficient clinical trial evidence to definitively determine the effectiveness of garlic in preventing or treating the common cold. While the single trial suggested that garlic might reduce the occurrence of colds, further high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings. Current claims of garlic's effectiveness are largely based on low-quality evidence.
